reading.rtitle: Keep It to Yourself? The Case For and Against Sharing Hidden Places
paras: Every time a travel writer publishes a list of hidden gems, somebody in a small village groans. The argument against these lists is simple, and I have some sympathy with it: the more people hear about a quiet place, the less quiet it becomes. Twenty years ago, the valley above Theth, in the Albanian Alps, saw a few hundred walkers a year. Today it sees far more than that in a single August week, and the guesthouses are nowhere near as cheap as they were. It is a fair point, and anyone who has watched a favorite beach disappear under umbrellas will find it hard to argue with.

But let me play devil's advocate. The claim that tourism simply ruins places is a sweeping generalization, and the people who make it rarely back it up with numbers. In the same valley, the money from visitors has kept a school open and brought young families back from the city. The village is not as untouched as it was, but it is considerably more alive. The question, then, is not whether people should come, but how. The slower the visitors travel, the more they spend locally, and the less damage they do.

This is the real bone of contention between travelers and the people who live where they travel, and I will not pretend to sit on the fence. I beg to differ with those who want to keep every good place a secret. The counterargument I hear most often is that a secret shared is a secret lost, and I concede that some places are much better off without a crowd. But a hidden place helps the few people who already know it, not the people who live there. On this, my readers and I may simply have to agree to disagree. Over the years, though, quite a few of them have come around to my view.
reading.source: Adapted from a travel opinion column by Fiona Reid

gapfill.text: This column runs on COMPARATIVES THAT MEASURE. THE + comparative, THE + comparative = two things change together: 'THE MORE people hear about it, THE LESS quiet it becomes.' NOWHERE NEAR AS ... AS = a big difference, in the negative: 'NOWHERE NEAR AS CHEAP AS it was.' FAR, MUCH, CONSIDERABLY + comparative = a big difference: 'FAR MORE walkers'. SLIGHTLY, A BIT + comparative = a small one.

bank.label: Useful language for a good argument
items: That is a fair point, but I see it differently.
I concede that the money helps the village.
With respect, I beg to differ.
Let me play devil's advocate for a minute.
The more I read about it, the less sure I am.
It is nowhere near as simple as it sounds.
Can you back that up with a real example?
I think we will have to agree to disagree.

lf.title: Which one? (blue = TWO things change TOGETHER)
items: The more I read about it

lf.text: A and C, in blue, use THE + comparative twice: two things change together, and both halves need THE. B and D measure ONE difference: NOWHERE NEAR AS ... AS makes it big in the negative, CONSIDERABLY makes it big in the positive. So ask yourself first: are two things moving together, or am I saying how big one difference is?

items: Compare Sao Paulo traffic today with twenty years ago. Use 'nowhere near as ... as' and 'far more'.
Finish three sentences: 'The more I ride, ...', 'The older I get, ...', 'The more podcasts I listen to, ...'.
A friend says: 'Tourism always ruins places.' Concede one point, then disagree, with one real example.
Give your honest opinion: should travelers share hidden places online? Use two comparatives that measure.

answerkey.title: Reveal the answer key
list: Gap-fill: 1 = the more, 2 = the less, 3 = nowhere near, 4 = far, 5 = considerably, 6 = the slower.
Model (Scenario 1): 'Traffic today is nowhere near as bad as it was in the nineties at night, but in the morning it is far worse.'
Model (Scenario 2): 'The more I ride, the better I sleep.' 'The older I get, the less I worry about speed.'
Model (Scenario 3): 'That is a fair point about prices, but I beg to differ. In one village I know, the visitors kept the school open.'
Shapes: the + comparative twice = change together. nowhere near as ... as = a big difference. far / much / considerably = big; slightly / a bit = small.
answerkey.note: Never use VERY with a comparative: 'very more crowded' is wrong. Say 'far more crowded' or 'much more crowded'.

listenings.text: Hi Marcelo, it is Fiona. Thank you for reading the column before it went out. I have had far more emails about this one than about anything I have written this year, and they are nowhere near as polite as yours. About half of the readers think I am completely wrong. One man wrote that the more I write about quiet places, the faster they disappear, and honestly, that is a fair point. But very few people back up their opinion with anything real. So here is my plan. I am going to write a second column, and this time I would like to quote a real traveler who has seen a place change. You have been riding these roads for fifteen years. Would you be willing to give me two or three sentences? Call me when you can.

Here is something most of us were never taught. How to disagree without losing a friend. First, find the part you agree with, and say it out loud. That is a fair point. You have a point there. People relax when they hear it, and the more relaxed they are, the more they listen. Second, avoid sweeping generalizations. Words like always and never make an argument sound far stronger than it is, and much easier to attack. Third, back up your claim with one real example, not ten. One good story is worth more than a page of numbers. And finally, know when to stop. If the conversation is going nowhere, you can simply agree to disagree. The goal of a good argument is not to win. It is to leave the table still friends.

extra_audio.text: First, Fiona admits the problem: the more people hear about a quiet place, the less quiet it becomes. Then she gives the example of the valley above Theth, which now sees far more walkers than twenty years ago. After that, she plays devil's advocate and says the claim that tourism ruins places is a sweeping generalization. Next, she shows that the money from visitors has made the village considerably more alive. Finally, she refuses to sit on the fence and accepts that some readers will have to agree to disagree.
